title.value: Autism incidence and spatial analysis in more than 7 million pupils in English schools: a retrospective, longitudinal, school registry study
title.justification: The title reflects the main focus and scope of the research conducted within the paper.
title.quote: Autism incidence and spatial analysis in more than 7 million pupils in English schools: a retrospective, longitudinal, school registry study

extractions.description: This study investigates the incidence of autism in English schools from 2014-2017, examining how geography, socioeconomic factors, and ethnic backgrounds influence autism diagnosis and the accessibility of diagnostic services.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The paper primarily focuses on autism incidence, spatial analysis, and socio-demographic factors. While these can indirectly relate to social sustainability in healthcare access, they do not directly address Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: Environmental and social factors might interact with autism aetiology. Speaking a language other than English and economic hardship might increase access barriers to autism diagnostic services, autism-specific Education, Health and Care Plans, and school-level support.

primary_category.justification: The paper concentrates on health access and autism diagnostics, without direct links to Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development, which are unrelated to the paper's core focus.
primary_category.quote: The incidence of autism varies across sex, age, ethnicity, and geographical location. Environmental and social factors might interact with autism aetiology.

secondary_categories.justification: Since the paper does not address multiple Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development areas, it does not have relevant secondary categories.
secondary_categories.quote: Our spatial analysis showed significant spatial autocorrelation across lower-layer super output areas in England, with 2338 hotspots (high-incidence areas surrounded by other high-incidence areas).

primary_sub_category.justification: The paper does not specifically fit into any of the sub-categories listed under Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development.
primary_sub_category.quote: To assess geographical, socioeconomic, and ethnic determinants of autism status in England, we present results from a large, longitudinal study of individuals with registered Special Education Needs and Disability (SEND).

secondary_sub_categories.justification: As the paper does not address multiple relevant areas within the framework of Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development, secondary sub-categories are not applicable.
secondary_sub_categories.quote: We conducted a large, retrospective, longitudinal, school registry study to investigate variation in autism incidence in England across different population strata (age, sex at birth, and ethnicity) and measures of family-level and area-level socioeconomic adversity.

applications.justification: Specific applications related to Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development are not discussed in the paper, which focuses on autism incidence and diagnostic access within educational settings.
applications.quote: Our main objective was to identify whether local variation in the incidence of autism is based on area-level and family-level social determinants of health.

new_primary_category.justification: The existing predefined categories do not include topics related to health access and autism incidence focusing on sociodemographic factors; therefore, a new category is not needed.
new_primary_category.quote: This study investigates the incidence of autism in England as a function of geography and sociodemographics, examining spatial distribution across health service boundaries.

new_primary_sub_category.justification: The paper does not necessitate the creation of a new sub-category since its topics fall outside the areas of Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development.
new_primary_sub_category.quote: We aimed to investigate the incidence of autism in England as a function of geography and sociodemographics, examining spatial distribution across health service boundaries.
